title: New Zealand's regions · GeoClick Geography
edition: Regions of Europe · one lesson per country · November 2026
intro: Welcome to New Zealand's regions, part 1 of 1. First, I clear the chosen names for a fresh regional lesson.
We work through 16 of the New Zealand regions the map names, once each: where it sits, one fact worth keeping, and a hook to remember it by.

states.name: Northland
lines: Northland fills the far north of the North Island, reaching out to Three Kings Bay, with its largest city, Whangarei, on the east coast and the Auckland region just below it.

The Treaty of Waitangi, which set out how the country would be shared between Māori and the British Crown, was signed at Waitangi in 1840, and every year the treaty flag is raised on the marae at the bay.
Remember the far north with the treaty grounds at the bay and the giant kauri standing in the Waipoua forest.

states.name: Auckland
lines: Auckland sits on the narrow neck of land in the north-east of the North Island, where its largest city straddles two harbours, with Northland to the north and Waikato to the south.
The city is built over the vents of about fifty small volcanoes, the highest of them Mount Eden, and it is the largest city in the country.
Remember the harbour city on a field of volcanoes, named for an English earl who never came here.

states.name: Waikato
lines: Waikato is the large inland region in the middle of the North Island, running from the Auckland border down to Taranaki and Hawke's Bay, with its largest city, Hamilton, in the centre.
The Shire from The Lord of the Rings was built for the film on a farm near Matamata, and the set was rebuilt in permanent timber and kept open.
Remember the flowing water that names the region, the longest river in the country, and the caves lit by thousands of glowworms.

states.name: Bay of Plenty
lines: Bay of Plenty runs along the east coast of the North Island, north of Hawke's Bay, with its largest city, Tauranga, on the shore and Gisborne at its far eastern corner.
Te Puke calls itself the kiwifruit capital of the world, and most of the kiwifruit shipped overseas is grown in this bay.
Remember the bay named for a feast, with the kiwifruit town inland and a smoking volcano out at sea.
states.transition: Let's bring Bay of Plenty into view.

states.name: Gisborne
lines: Gisborne is the far north-eastern corner of the North Island, facing the Pacific, with its largest city of the same name and Hawke's Bay to the south.
Captain Cook came ashore in New Zealand here in 1769, and the town was named in 1870 for William Gisborne, a colonial official in London.
Remember the place where the sun comes up among the first in the world, and where Cook first set foot on New Zealand.

states.name: Taranaki
lines: Taranaki is the small region on the west coast of the North Island, between Waikato and Manawatū-Whanganui, with its largest city, New Plymouth, on the shore.
The mountain that gives the region its name, which Captain Cook renamed Mount Egmont in 1770, is an almost perfect volcanic cone 2,518 metres high.
Remember the perfect cone on the west coast, the one that doubled for Mount Fuji in a film.

states.name: Hawke's Bay
lines: Hawke's Bay is on the east coast of the North Island, with its largest city, Hastings, inland from the shore, sitting south of Gisborne and north of the Wellington region.
Napier was destroyed by a strong earthquake in 1931 and rebuilt in the Art Deco style, so the centre still looks like the 1930s.
Remember the bay named for an admiral and the earthquake town rebuilt in deco style.
states.transition: Let's bring Hawke's Bay into view.

states.name: Manawatū-Whanganui
lines: Manawatū-Whanganui is the inland region in the middle of the North Island, between Taranaki on the west and Hawke's Bay on the east, with its largest city, Palmerston North, in the south and the snow-capped Mount Ruapehu in the far south of it.
In 2017 the Whanganui River was recognised in court as a living being, the first river in the world to be given the legal rights of a person.
Remember the region named after two rivers, one of which counts as a person in law.

states.name: Wellington
lines: Wellington is the region at the southern tip of the North Island, with the capital city of the same name on its harbour and Manawatū-Whanganui to the north.
Te Papa, the national museum, stands on the waterfront, and its name comes from the Māori words for the world of the ancestors.
Remember the windy capital at the foot of the North Island, named for the duke who won at Waterloo.

states.name: Nelson
lines: Nelson is the small region at the top of the South Island, on the north coast between Tasman and Marlborough, with its largest city of the same name at the shore.
It claims to be one of the sunniest places in New Zealand, and the World of WearableArt, a show of costumes made as art, began here in 1987.
Remember the sunny corner at the top of the South Island, named for the admiral who died at Trafalgar.

states.name: Tasman
lines: Tasman is the region across the top of the South Island, west of Nelson and Marlborough, running down the coast to Canterbury, with no large city of its own.
It is named for Abel Tasman, the Dutch explorer who sighted New Zealand in 1642, and the long curve of Farewell Spit reaches out into the sea at its northern corner.
Remember the long sand spit sweeping into the sea at the top of the island, named for the Dutch sailor who first sighted the country.

states.name: Marlborough
lines: Marlborough is the region at the north-east of the South Island, with its largest city, Blenheim, in the north and the maze of the Marlborough Sounds at the top of the island.
It is by far New Zealand's biggest wine region, and most of the sauvignon blanc the country exports is grown here.
Remember the drowned valleys of the Sounds and the region that grows the country's wine.

states.name: West Coast
lines: West Coast is the long thin region on the western side of the South Island, running from Tasman in the north down to Fiordland in the south, with its largest city, Greymouth, on the coast.
The gold rush of the 1860s brought thousands of diggers to its rivers, and the town of Charleston keeps the old miners' cottages on its main street.
Remember the narrow western strip where the glaciers come down almost to the rainforest by the sea.
states.transition: Let's bring West Coast into view.

states.name: Canterbury
lines: Canterbury fills the middle of the east coast of the South Island, spreading from the Marlborough border and the snowy Southern Alps down over the flat plains to Otago, with its largest city, Christchurch, on the shore.
Aoraki, or Mount Cook, 3,724 metres, the highest mountain in New Zealand, rises in the Southern Alps at the head of the Canterbury region.
Remember the plains and the snow peak behind them, and the city that was rebuilt after the earthquakes.

states.name: Otago
lines: Otago lies in the south-west of the South Island, between Canterbury and Southland, reaching out to the Otago Peninsula and the city of Dunedin on the east coast.
Dunedin was founded in 1848 by Scottish Free Church settlers and was nicknamed the Edinburgh of the South, and its university, founded in 1869, is the oldest in the country.
Remember the Scottish city of Dunedin, with albatrosses nesting at Taiaroa Head on its peninsula.

states.name: Southland
lines: Southland is the southernmost region of the South Island, below Otago and the West Coast, with its largest city, Invercargill, in the south and Fiordland along its western side.
Fiordland, which lies largely within the region, holds Milford Sound, one of the wettest places in the country, where waterfalls drop straight into the sea.
Remember the very bottom of the island, and the wild kiwi of Stewart Island, or Rakiura, that can be seen in daylight.

recap: 16 regions of New Zealand, one for each target of the map: Northland, Auckland, Waikato, Bay of Plenty, Gisborne, Taranaki, Hawke's Bay, Manawatū-Whanganui, Wellington, Nelson, Tasman, Marlborough, West Coast, Canterbury, Otago and Southland.
Remember the shape of New Zealand from the inside: the regions nest around each other, and every name on the map belongs somewhere in this one country.
